item.research_question: How can elemental partitioning-mediated crystalline-to-amorphous phase transformation be realized under quasi-static deformation to achieve ultrahigh strength and large plasticity in a crystal-glass nanolaminated composite?
item.material_system: Cr-Ni-Co (crystalline)/Zr-Ti-Nb-Hf-Ni-Co (amorphous) nanolaminated composite; specific compositions: Cr35Ni33Co32 (at.%) and Zr28Ti24Nb22Hf19Ni6Co1 (at.%)
item.processing_route: Magnetron sputtering with alternate deposition of CrCoNi and TiZrNbHf targets; substrate temperature below 50 °C; Ar working pressure 4 × 10−3 mbar; deposition rates 3 nm/min (CrCoNi) and 5 nm/min (TiZrNbHf); layer thicknesses 17.0 nm (crystalline) and 6.7 nm (amorphous)
item.test_conditions: Quasi-static pillar compression at strain rates of ~2 × 10−3 s−1; in-situ TEM cyclic loading-unloading compression; micro-indentation for ex-situ TEM and APT analysis
key_findings: The crystal-glass nanolaminated alloy exhibits a yield strength of 3.7 GPa and homogeneous plastic deformation of ~20% strain in compression.

The crystalline Cr-Ni-Co phase transforms into an amorphous phase upon plastic deformation, confirmed by a drastic reduction in crystalline diffraction spots and the appearance of an amorphous halo ring in SAED.
Elemental partitioning occurs during deformation, with Ni, Co, and Cr contents in the original Zr-rich region increasing from 6 at.%, 1 at.%, 0 at.% to 35 at.%, 25 at.%, 20 at.%.
The radius of the amorphous halo ring in SAED increases after deformation, indicating a change in short-range-order (SRO) structure towards the atomic packing of the Cr, Ni, Co-enriched phase.
The amorphous nanodomains formed have a size below 10 nm, which promotes homogeneous plastic flow and prevents shear band formation.
The material shows strain hardening up to ~22% true strain, contrasting with the strain softening or shear banding observed in reference crystalline and amorphous alloys.
item.mechanism: The authors propose that extensive rearrangement of atoms at the crystal-glass interfaces during deformation facilitates elemental partitioning due to the large negative mixing enthalpy among constituent elements. This intermixing transforms the original crystalline phase into an amorphous phase (CA-TRIP). The dislocations emitted from the interface are absorbed by the amorphous phase, and the massive atomic rearrangement induces this phase transformation. The resulting nanodomained amorphous structure with different compositions impedes shear band propagation, enabling global strain hardening and homogeneous plastic flow.
item.limitations: The deviation of stress-strain curves after ~20% strain originates from mechanical instability of the pillar sample during inhomogeneous deformation. The study notes that the CA-TRIP phenomenon does not appear in CuZr/Cu systems due to reduced negative mixing enthalpy from high Cu content.
item.future_work: The authors suggest this enthalpy-guided alloy design strategy provides guidelines for developing dual-phase alloys and may find applications in load-bearing micro-electro-mechanical systems and protective surface coatings.
quotes: Upon plastic deformation, atomic intermixing occurs between adjacent amorphous and crystalline phases due to extensive rearrangement of atoms at the interfaces.
The large negative mixing enthalpy among the constituent elements promotes amorphous phase transformation of the original crystalline phase.
The massive rearrangement of atoms at the interfaces facilitates the elemental partitioning behavior between the adjacent phases, inducing the CA-TRIP effect.
